questions.prompt: Why is a single instance of "whoami /all" or "systeminfo" in a log usually NOT enough to flag as suspicious on its own?
options: These commands never appear in real intrusions
Administrators run these same commands routinely for legitimate reasons — the signal is in who ran it, from where, and what surrounds it
Windows blocks these commands by default
They only matter if run by a Domain Admin account
questions.explanation: The baseline explicitly isn't "this command never appears" — it's the context: account history, timing, and clustering with other discovery commands.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson call out nltest /domain_trusts as unusually high-signal compared to the other four commands?
options: It's the only one that requires Domain Admin rights to even run
It's a genuinely uncommon command for anyone other than a domain administrator, making it high-signal even in isolation
It doesn't map to any MITRE ATT&CK technique
It's the only command that gets logged by default
questions.explanation: Unlike whoami or systeminfo, which routine admin work generates constantly, nltest /domain_trusts is rare enough outside dedicated AD administration to be meaningfully high-signal on its own.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that "Discovery is iterative"?
options: It only happens once, at the very start of an intrusion
The same discovery-command pattern repeats at every new foothold as an attacker moves through an environment — useful for scoping lateral movement
Discovery commands must be run in a specific fixed order
It refers to Windows automatically repeating logged events
questions.explanation: A real intrusion repeats the discovery pattern at each new host — seeing it recur across multiple systems in sequence traces the attacker's actual path.

questions.prompt: What log source is required to distinguish "whoami" from "whoami /all" in Windows process-creation logging?
options: No special configuration is needed — arguments are always logged
Command-line auditing must be explicitly enabled, or only the process name is visible with no argument detail
questions.explanation: Without the "Include command line in process creation events" policy enabled, Event ID 4688 shows only the process name — arguments (and therefore the /all flag) are invisible.
